nature-econ-461.title: Optimization: the mathematics of choosing the best
nature-econ-461.text: Every economic choice is a hunt for the best option among those on offer. One influential definition calls economics the study of human behavior as a relationship between ends and scarce means that have alternative uses. Mathematical optimization is the formal version of that hunt: choosing the best option, judged by some criterion, from a set of available alternatives. In practice it usually means making a function as large or as small as possible by choosing inputs from an allowed set. A function here is simply a rule that turns inputs into an output. Some problems are discrete, with the answer drawn from a countable set such as the whole numbers. Others are continuous. Economists lean on optimization constantly. Consumers are usually assumed to maximize utility and firms to maximize profit. Utility maximization has a mirror-image twin, expenditure minimization, and both are standard examples. Since the 1970s economists have also modeled decisions that unfold over time with control theory. The tools are old. Fermat and Lagrange found calculus-based formulas for the best point, while Newton and Gauss proposed step-by-step methods for moving toward one. Optimization problems now arise in every quantitative field, from engineering to operations research. Even the vocabulary has a story: the 'programming' in {{ref:nature-econ-456}} comes from the US military's word for training and logistics schedules, not from computer programming.

nature-econ-429.title: The derivative: how fast things change right now
nature-econ-429.text: How fast is something changing at this exact moment? The derivative answers that question. It measures how sensitive a function's output is to a small change in its input. For a function of one variable, it is the slope of the tangent line at a point, the straight line that just grazes the curve there. That tangent is the best straight-line approximation of the function near the point. The derivative is often described as the instantaneous rate of change, and finding it is called differentiation. Formally, it is the limit of the ratio of change in output to change in input as the input change shrinks to zero. A function must be continuous at a point to have a derivative there, so a sudden step jump has none. Rules for sums, products and compositions let the derivative of a complicated function be built from those of simple pieces. Gottfried Wilhelm Leibniz introduced the notation still used today, dy/dx, in 1675. Economists use the idea all the time. Short-run marginal cost is the slope, or first derivative, of the variable cost curve.

nature-econ-433.title: Differential equations: laws written as rates of change
nature-econ-433.text: Many laws of nature are statements about how fast things change. A differential equation captures such a law: it links one or more unknown functions to their derivatives, that is, to their rates of change ({{ref:nature-econ-429}}). These equations arose with the invention of calculus by Isaac Newton and Gottfried Leibniz, and Newton listed three kinds in a 1671 work. Today they model almost every physical, technical or biological process, from celestial motion to bridge design to neurons. Because such relations run through scientific models, differential equations are prominent in engineering, physics, economics and biology. The catch is that only the simplest can be solved by an explicit formula. Many properties of the solutions can still be found without solving them exactly. When no formula exists, computers can approximate the solutions numerically. The theory of dynamical systems studies qualitative features of the solutions, such as their average long-run behavior. There are limits, though. A system of many interacting, adapting parts may have so many elements that a system of differential equations becomes impractical and stops helping anyone understand it.

nature-econ-442.title: Exponential growth: the bigger it gets, the faster it grows
nature-econ-442.text: A bacterium that doubles every ten minutes becomes 64 bacteria after one hour. That is exponential growth: a quantity increasing at a rate proportional to its current size, so the bigger it gets, the faster it grows. Something three times bigger is growing three times as fast. The usual illustration is a bacterium splitting into 2, then 4, 8, 16 and 32. Exponential growth is not the same as rapid growth, because it can be slow at first. Economics is full of it. Economic growth is stated in percentages, which implies exponential growth, and {{ref:nature-econ-781}} at a constant rate grows capital exponentially. Run the process with a negative rate and the quantity shrinks instead, which is exponential decay. Over the long run, exponential growth overtakes any linear growth, growth by a fixed amount each period. That gap is the basis of the Malthusian catastrophe. Malthus warned that population growing geometrically, doubling every 25 years, would outrun food production growing arithmetically. Yet real exponential growth rarely lasts. External limits eventually slow it into {{ref:nature-eco-580}}.

nature-econ-423.title: Constrained optimization: the best choice within limits
nature-econ-423.text: Nobody gets to choose without limits. Constrained optimization finds the best value of an objective, such as a cost to minimize or a utility to maximize. The catch is that the choices must obey constraints, rules they cannot break. It is {{ref:nature-econ-461}} with fences. Hard constraints must be met. Soft constraints may be broken, but each violation is penalized in the objective in proportion to how far it goes. Consumer theory models a buyer's demand on exactly this hypothesis, with the {{ref:nature-econ-102}} as the fence. In a typical model of spending over time, discounted utility is maximized subject to one rule: the present value of spending cannot exceed the present value of resources. Mathematicians have a tool for each case. With only equality constraints, {{ref:nature-econ-455}} turns the problem into an unconstrained one, with one extra variable per constraint. With inequality constraints, the {{ref:nature-econ-452}} generalize that method, provided the functions are smooth and suitably bowl-shaped. If the objective and all constraints are linear, the problem is {{ref:nature-econ-456}}. If any of them are nonlinear, it is {{ref:nature-econ-425}}.

nature-econ-427.title: Convex functions: why cup-shaped curves are easy to optimize
nature-econ-427.text: A convex function is one whose graph lies on or below the straight line joining any two of its points, so the graph is cup-shaped. A concave function is cap-shaped, and a function f is convex exactly when its negative, −f, is concave. For a smooth function of one variable, convexity means the second derivative, the rate of change of the slope, is never negative ({{ref:nature-econ-429}}). Linear functions, quadratics like cx² with c not negative, and exponentials like ceˣ with c not negative are all convex. Any local minimum of a convex function, a low point in its own neighborhood, is also the global minimum. Jensen's inequality adds that a convex function of an average is never more than the average of the function's values. Economists meet the idea constantly. A diminishing marginal rate of substitution along an indifference curve means preferences are convex, and demand curves are generally considered convex, in line with diminishing marginal utility.

nature-econ-456.title: Linear programming: planning with straight-line rules
nature-econ-456.text: A farmer with limited land, fertilizer and pesticide must choose how many hectares of wheat and barley to plant for the most revenue. Linear programming finds the best outcome, such as maximum profit or lowest cost, when the goal and all the requirements are linear relationships, with no curves. It is a special case of {{ref:nature-econ-423}}. The inequalities cut out the set of allowed choices, a many-sided shape called a convex polytope. Leonid Kantorovich and Wassily Leontief independently explored its practical uses in the late 1930s. Kantorovich later shared the 1975 Nobel Memorial Prize in Economic Sciences with T. C. Koopmans. George B. Dantzig developed the general formulation in 1946–1947 for US Air Force planning and invented the {{ref:nature-econ-457}} in 1947. The method shaped early microeconomics and helped inspire key ideas in optimization, such as {{ref:nature-econ-438}} and the importance of convexity. The earliest precursor of the DICE climate-economy model built by {{ref:nature-hist-050}} was a linear programming model of energy supply and demand from 1977.

nature-econ-437.title: Discrete and continuous time: steps or a smooth flow
nature-econ-437.text: A digital clock jumps from 10:37 to 10:38 with nothing in between. That is discrete time: a variable is fixed within each period and jumps between periods. Continuous time instead lets time range over the real numbers, so infinitely many moments lie between any two points in time. Economists use both. Economic activity happens continuously but can only be measured in steps, which is why GDP data come as a series of quarterly values. Discrete time suits empirical work and time series models. Continuous-time theoretical models are often easier to handle mathematically. Each comes with its own tools: discrete time uses {{ref:nature-econ-436}}, while continuous time uses differential equations. The total discounted utility from a stream of consumption is a sum in discrete time and an integral, a continuous sum, in continuous time.

nature-econ-474.title: Steady state: when everything flows but nothing changes
nature-econ-474.text: A system is in steady state when its defining variables are not changing over time. Things may still flow through it, but nothing builds up or runs down. In continuous time the rate of change of each property is zero; in discrete time each period-to-period difference is zero ({{ref:nature-econ-437}}). Many systems pass through a transient, warm-up period first, and often only approach steady state gradually. In a simple model that tracks an element moving between stores in the environment, a store is in steady state when its sources balance its sinks. Economics uses the same idea. In the Solow–Swan growth model, the steady state arrives when gross investment in physical capital equals depreciation, the wearing out of existing capital. Growth models without technological change predict that economies converge to a steady state with zero growth per person. In the sense of {{ref:nature-eecon-072}}, an economy in steady state has a stable population and stable consumption at or below {{ref:nature-eco-593}}. Not every steady state holds, though: an unstable system moves away from it.

nature-econ-421.title: Calculus of variations: finding the best whole curve
nature-econ-421.text: What is the shortest curve joining two points? With no constraints the answer is a straight line, but proving it takes a special branch of mathematics. The calculus of variations finds the functions that make a functional as large or as small as possible. A functional maps a whole function to a single number, so functionals have been described as functions of functions. They are often written as definite integrals, sums over a whole range. The method mirrors ordinary {{ref:nature-econ-461}}. A function's maxima and minima lie where its derivative is zero; a functional's extremes lie where its functional derivative is zero, which leads to the {{ref:nature-econ-422}}. The field began with Isaac Newton's minimal resistance problem, solved in 1685, and his 1697 solution of the brachistochrone problem. In economics, optimization over time has used the calculus of variations, following Frank P. Ramsey and {{ref:nature-hist-062}}.

nature-econ-475.title: Computable general equilibrium: modeling a whole economy
nature-econ-475.text: A tax on flour might raise bread prices, lift the consumer price index, and then ripple into wages and employment. Computable general equilibrium (CGE) models trace such chains. They use real economic data to estimate how a whole economy might respond to changes in policy, technology or other outside factors. A CGE model is a set of equations plus a detailed database consistent with them, usually assuming cost-minimizing producers and optimizing households ({{ref:nature-econ-382}}). Their ancestor is the {{ref:nature-acct-080}}, but unlike it they let prices matter, so a wage rise can change how much labor is used to make bread. They have been used widely for trade policy and, more recently, to estimate the economic effects of cutting the gases that warm the climate. For climate policy they can show gains and losses across households with different incomes or in different regions. Many are comparative static: they compare the economy with and without a policy shock at one future point, without modeling the path between. They work where time-series data are scarce, so developing economies are often analyzed with them.

nature-econ-430.title: Partial derivatives: changing one thing at a time
nature-econ-430.text: Many quantities depend on several inputs at once. A partial derivative isolates one of them. It is the derivative of a function of several variables with respect to one variable, holding the others fixed ({{ref:nature-econ-429}}). It can be read as the function's rate of change in the direction of that one variable. Partial derivatives therefore measure change only along the coordinate axes. Change in other directions is measured by directional derivatives. The total derivative gives the complete picture by considering all directions at once.

nature-econ-436.title: Difference equations: change in separate steps
nature-econ-436.text: Not everything changes smoothly. A difference equation relates a quantity's value at one point to its values at nearby points, when time or another variable takes only separate values. Also called recurrence relations, difference equations are the discrete-time counterpart of {{ref:nature-econ-433}} ({{ref:nature-econ-437}}). The two can stand in for each other. Numerical methods such as the Euler method approximate a differential equation by a matching difference equation. An economist can model a price adjusting to excess demand, buyers wanting more than sellers offer, either way. Ecology has a matched pair too: the Beverton–Holt population model is a discrete-time analogue of Verhulst's continuous-time equation for {{ref:nature-eco-580}}.

nature-econ-450.title: Integer programming: when answers must be whole numbers
nature-econ-450.text: It is not possible to build 3.7 cars. Integer programming handles choices like that: optimization in which some or all of the choice variables must be whole numbers. It usually means integer linear programming, where the objective and other constraints are linear ({{ref:nature-econ-456}}). If only some variables must be whole, it is mixed-integer programming. Integers also code yes-or-no decisions as 0 or 1. A farm can use it to plan yields for several crops that share land, labor, capital, seeds and fertilizer, maximizing production without exceeding resources. Districting problems, including waste management districting, are solved this way while respecting natural boundaries and contiguity. The difficulty is that integer programming is NP-complete, a class of problems with no known fast general method, so many instances are intractable. Exact methods include cutting planes and variants of {{ref:nature-econ-426}}. Heuristic shortcuts such as tabu search handle the rest.

nature-eco-580.title: Logistic growth: fast at first, then leveling off
nature-eco-580.text: Malthus described population growing without limit. The Belgian mathematician Pierre François Verhulst read Malthus's Essay on the Principle of Population and adjusted the picture. Logistic growth starts out exponential ({{ref:nature-econ-442}}) but slows as it approaches an upper limit set by external or environmental factors. A population, for instance, may level off because resources run short. Verhulst devised the model between 1838 and 1847 and first proposed it in 1845. It arises when self-limiting effects, the brakes ignored in the exponential model, become significant. In ecology it is a differential equation, dP/dt = rP(1 − P/K), where P is the population, r the growth rate and K the {{ref:nature-eco-593}}. As the population grows, competition for critical resources slows growth until the population stops growing at K. The discrete-time Beverton–Holt population model is its step-by-step analogue.

nature-econ-417.title: State and control variables: where things stand, what to choose
nature-econ-417.text: Someone deciding how much to spend over the years juggles two kinds of quantity. Wealth is the state: the information about the current situation needed to choose well. How much to consume now is the control variable: what the decision-maker chooses at each moment. Like every optimization problem ({{ref:nature-econ-461}}), this one has an objective, such as minimizing cost or maximizing profit, described by a mathematical objective function. The two kinds are tightly linked. Choosing the controls now may amount to choosing the next state, though other factors usually affect the next state as well.

nature-econ-465.title: Optimal control: steering a system over time
nature-econ-465.text: How should a spacecraft reach the Moon on the least fuel? How should a government use fiscal and monetary policy to keep unemployment as low as possible? Both are optimal control problems. This branch of control theory finds how to steer a system that changes over time so that an objective is optimized over a whole period. It extends the {{ref:nature-econ-421}}, and Lev Pontryagin and Richard Bellman developed it mainly in the 1950s. Mining supplies a classic case. A mine owner chooses how fast to extract ore over the period of ownership to maximize profit, when extraction costs rise with speed. The best path can be found from {{ref:nature-econ-469}}, a necessary condition, or by solving the {{ref:nature-econ-470}}, a sufficient one. Most optimal control problems are nonlinear with no exact solution, so numerical methods are needed. Finding the best strategy in a differential game is a closely related task.

nature-econ-440.title: Dynamic programming: solving big decisions in small steps
nature-econ-440.text: Some big decisions break neatly into small ones. Dynamic programming exploits that. It solves a complex problem by breaking it recursively into simpler subproblems, and it is both an optimization method and a style of computer algorithm. Richard Bellman developed it in the 1950s, and it is used in fields such as aerospace engineering and economics. Decisions that span several points in time often break apart this way, though some problems cannot. The relation between the value of the whole problem and the values of its pieces is called the {{ref:nature-econ-416}}. Values are found by working backward from the last period, computing each earlier period's value from the next one. Computer scientists say it needs two features, optimal substructure and overlapping subproblems. Without the overlap, the approach is called divide and conquer. It is widely used in bioinformatics too, for sequence alignment and protein folding.

nature-econ-464.title: Multi-objective optimization: juggling goals that conflict
nature-econ-464.text: Many choices chase more than one goal. Multi-objective optimization handles problems where conflicting goals force a {{ref:nature-econ-099}}. A design is Pareto optimal if no other design is better on one criterion without being worse on another. The best trade-offs trace out the Pareto frontier. Mathematics can find that frontier, but choosing a point on it is left to the decision-maker, because how to weigh the goals is missing information. Portfolio optimization is an economic example.

nature-econ-432.title: Antiderivatives: running differentiation in reverse
nature-econ-432.text: Differentiation can be run backward. An antiderivative of a function is another function whose derivative is the given one ({{ref:nature-econ-429}}). Antiderivatives are not unique: adding any constant gives another, because a constant's derivative is zero. Their great use comes from the fundamental theorem of calculus. The integral of a function over an interval equals the difference between an antiderivative's values at the two ends, and that gives the area under a curve.

nature-econ-431.title: Higher-order derivatives: the rate of change of a rate
nature-econ-431.text: A derivative is itself a function, so it can be differentiated again ({{ref:nature-econ-429}}). Repeating the process gives higher-order derivatives. The derivative of the derivative is the second derivative, and the nth derivative is the derivative of the (n−1)th. The second derivative carries a useful message about shape. A twice-differentiable function of one variable is convex exactly when its second derivative is never negative ({{ref:nature-econ-427}}).

nature-econ-462.title: Optimality conditions: testing whether an answer is best
nature-econ-462.text: How can anyone tell that a candidate answer really is the best? Optimality conditions are the tests it must pass. By one of Fermat's theorems, the best points of an unconstrained problem lie at stationary points, where the first derivative, or gradient, is zero. There the curve is momentarily flat. Setting the derivative to zero is the first-order condition. More generally, the best point can also sit where the derivative is undefined, or on the boundary of the choice set. A flat spot could be a peak or a valley, and the first derivative cannot tell which. Second-order conditions can. Checking the second derivative ({{ref:nature-econ-431}}), or its many-variable version, the Hessian matrix, tells maxima from minima. Weierstrass's extreme value theorem guarantees there is something to find. A continuous function on a compact set, one that is closed and bounded, reaches both a maximum and a minimum.

nature-econ-455.title: Lagrange multipliers: pricing the constraints
nature-econ-455.text: Named after the mathematician Joseph-Louis Lagrange, this method finds the highest or lowest value of a function when the choices must satisfy one or more equations exactly. Its trick is a new function, the Lagrangian, that folds the constraints into the objective. The ordinary derivative test for unconstrained problems then works ({{ref:nature-econ-462}}). At the constrained optimum, the gradient of the objective is a linear combination of the constraints' gradients. Each multiplier also carries economic meaning. It measures how fast the optimized quantity changes as its constraint is relaxed. That is why economists reach for the method so often. In general equilibrium models, consumers maximize utility and firms maximize profit under budget and production constraints, usually solved with Lagrange multipliers. In optimal control the multipliers turn into the time-varying values of {{ref:nature-econ-466}}.

nature-econ-446.title: The Hamiltonian: a compass for optimal control
nature-econ-446.text: Lev Pontryagin needed one function that could guide a system steered over time. The Hamiltonian is that function. It is built to solve an {{ref:nature-econ-465}} problem, combining the objective with the equations that describe how the system's state changes. It was inspired by, but differs from, the Hamiltonian of classical mechanics. It works like a Lagrangian in static optimization ({{ref:nature-econ-455}}), except that its multipliers change over time ({{ref:nature-econ-466}}). Pontryagin proved a necessary condition for optimal control: the control must be chosen to optimize the Hamiltonian at each moment. The equations for the state and for those multipliers together form a two-point boundary value problem, with conditions at both the start and end times. In effect, the Hamiltonian is a device for generating the first-order conditions of a dynamic problem. A sufficient condition for a maximum is that the Hamiltonian be concave at the solution.

nature-econ-438.title: Duality: every optimization problem has a mirror image
nature-econ-438.text: Every optimization problem has a twin. Duality is the principle that any such problem can be viewed from two sides: the original, or primal, problem and a matching dual problem. If the primal is a minimization, the dual is a maximization, and vice versa. The two bound each other. Any feasible value of a primal minimization is at least as large as any feasible value of its dual. The usual dual adds the constraints to the objective using non-negative Lagrange multipliers ({{ref:nature-econ-455}}), which become the dual variables. Each constraint thus has its own dual variable, which later chapters meet as a {{ref:nature-val-017}}. Microeconomics has a famous pair: minimizing the spending needed to reach a level of happiness is the dual of maximizing utility. John von Neumann conjectured the duality theorem of linear programming, drawing on his game theory. Albert W. Tucker's group published the first rigorous proofs in 1948.

nature-econ-435.title: Initial conditions: where a system starts
nature-econ-435.text: A differential equation usually has many solutions, not one. The general solution of an nth-order ordinary differential equation, one with derivatives up to the nth, contains n undetermined constants. Initial conditions are the extra information, such as a system's starting values, that pin down which solution applies ({{ref:nature-econ-433}}). For a moving particle, they are usually its position and velocity at the starting time.

nature-econ-434.title: Kinds of differential equations and why they matter
nature-econ-434.text: Differential equations come in families, and the family helps guide the choice of solution method ({{ref:nature-econ-433}}). An ordinary differential equation has an unknown function of one variable. A partial differential equation has unknown functions of several variables and their partial derivatives ({{ref:nature-econ-430}}). The order is the highest derivative that appears; equations describing nature usually have only first and second derivatives. Equations are also linear or nonlinear, homogeneous or not. Linear ones have a well-developed theory. Few nonlinear ones can be solved exactly, and they can behave chaotically over long times.

openers.mathematical-tools-for-economics: Economics is the science of choosing well under limits, and mathematics gives that choosing a precise language. At its heart lies optimization: picking the best option, judged by some criterion, from the alternatives available, often while obeying constraints such as a cost or a budget. Calculus supplies the basic instrument, a measure of how sensitive an output is to a small change in an input, and equations built from these rates of change describe systems that evolve over time. Some quantities grow at a rate proportional to their size, so the bigger they get, the faster they grow, while others settle into a state where nothing changes. This chapter gathers these tools, from simple linear planning models to whole-economy models that use real data to estimate how policy changes ripple outward.
